top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore) credits a single, well-bounded mechanism, collateral-amplification of shocks into credit cycles, that is about thirty years old and was tested by 2007-09. It is now part of the shared core of macro, finance and policy modelling. Attribution is the cleanest on the slate, and a citation limited to collateral and balance-sheet amplification keeps it distinct from the 2022 banking prize. Its weaknesses are real: the specific collateral channel is only mixed-identified empirically, and the pair omits Gertler and Gilchrist. I rank P002 (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) a close second. It is a compact, mature method with a longer validated record in use, but it leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, and its counterfactuals depend on functional-form assumptions. The P001 margin is small and rests on weighting breadth of conceptual influence. P003 follows because the technology and trade strands, the overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes, and the shift-share inference debate leave its unit of recognition less sharp. No award ranks last because all three proposals are mature, credible achievements.
recusal_note: No documented tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes, Autor, Dorn or Hanson in my profile. I have co-authored with chair Hassler (a P001 supporter) and former chair Ellingsen (IJIO 2026). My field, industrial organisation, is closest to P002, my second choice, and I applied the same criteria across fields. I am an SSE colleague of other members. As a public fact only, my spouse is a Swedish politician; the profile shows no bearing on any candidate. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
